en: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Sañjaya, what did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do when they had assembled on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, desiring to fight?
Saṃjaya said:
Then, having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
"Behold, O Teacher, this vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
arrayed by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
Herein are heroes, great archers, equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle."
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic King of Kāśī;
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, the bull among men.
Yudhāmanyu the valiant, the heroic Uttamaujas,
the son of Subhadrā, and the sons of Draupadī— all of them are indeed great chariot-warriors (mahāratha).
But as for those among us who are distinguished, learn of them, O best of the twice-born.
I shall name to you those leaders of my army for your information:
yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, who is victorious in assembly,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta.
And many other heroes, who have renounced their lives for my sake,
equipped with various weapons and missiles, all skilled in battle—
that army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is not insufficient.
This force, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient for them; therefore,
all of you, stationed in your respective positions at all the flanks,
must protect Bhīṣma alone.
Then the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus, generating joy in him,
let out a lion’s roar and blew his conch shell loudly.
Thereupon, conch shells, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns [resounded].
Suddenly they were struck together, and that sound became tumultuous. Then, standing upon a great chariot yoked with white horses,
Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava blew their divine conch shells.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya; Dhanañjaya blew the Devadatta;
Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra;
and King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya.
Nakula and Sahadeva, Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka, the king of Kāśī with his supreme bow, and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki.
O lord of the earth, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī,
and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conchs individually;
that sound rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Making both the sky and the earth resound with a tumultuous noise,
the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the monkey, then raised his bow as the Dhārtarāṣṭras stood arrayed and the clash of weapons was about to begin.
Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies,
so that I may behold those who stand here desiring to fight."
With whom must I fight in this military undertaking? I shall observe those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for battle.
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa,
having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies,
in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and all the lords of the earth, [said:]
He said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here.
There, Pārtha saw standing his fathers, grandfathers,
teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
Having beheld all those kinsmen standing in both armies— fathers-in-law and friends alike— that son of Kuntī,
overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, spoke as follows.
O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here desiring to fight,
my limbs fail me and my mouth becomes parched;
trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end.
The *Gāṇḍīva* bow slips from my hand and my skin is burning all over; I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to be reeling. Moreover, O Keśava, I behold portents that are adverse.
And I do not perceive any good in slaying my own kin in battle. I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor sovereignty, nor pleasures.
Of what use is sovereignty to us, O Govinda, or of what use are enjoyments or even life itself?
For whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
these very ones stand here in battle, having abandoned their lives and wealth:
teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers.
Uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen—
these I do not wish to kill, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me,
not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, much less for the sake of the earth.
"O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us in slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
By killing these aggressors, only sin would take hold of us. Therefore, we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kinsmen."
For how, O Mādhava, could we be happy after killing our own kin?
Even though these men, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil resulting from the destruction of the family, nor the sin in betraying friends.

O Janārdana, how could we not recognize that we must turn away from this sin, when we clearly perceive the evil resulting from the destruction of the lineage? With the destruction of the family, the eternal family traditions perish.
When dharma is destroyed, adharma overcomes the entire family.
O Kṛṣṇa, through the prevalence of adharma, the women of the family become corrupted.
When the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, there arises an intermixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara).
The confusion of castes leads only to hell for both the destroyers of the family and the family itself;
indeed, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
By these faults of the family-destroyers, which cause the intermixture of castes, [the world is afflicted].
The eternal laws of caste and family traditions are destroyed;
O Janārdana, we have heard from tradition that for those men whose family traditions are destroyed, residence in hell is inevitable.

"Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty we are prepared to slay our own kin. If those with weapons in hand were to kill me, unresisting and unarmed,"
"It would be better for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were to slay me in battle.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot,
casting aside his bow and arrow, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Saṃjaya said:
To him who was thus overcome with compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears,
and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
The Blessed One said:
"O Arjuna, whence has come upon you this dejection in this hour of peril? It is un-Aryan, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy."
"Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe!
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight against Bhīṣma and Droṇa with my arrows in battle, for they are both worthy of honor? Indeed,
it would be better not to slay these high-souled elders.
It is better to live on alms in this world than to slay these venerable elders for the sake of wealth and pleasure,
and thus enjoy riches stained with blood.
Nor do we know which is better for us:
whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us;
for we have no desire to live even after having slain those very people.
Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand arrayed before me;
my own nature is overwhelmed by the defect of compassion,
and with my mind confused about duty, I ask you.
Tell me decisively which of these two is better;
I am your disciple, teach me who have taken refuge in you.
For I do not perceive [any path] that might dispel my grief.
Having obtained on earth unrivaled and prosperous sovereignty, even the lordship over the gods, that which withers the senses with grief— [that sovereignty].
Saṃjaya said:
Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes,
said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent.
O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies. The Blessed Lord said:
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not grieve for the dead or the living.
Indeed, at no time was I non-existent, nor were you, nor these lords of men.

And yet, none of us shall cease to exist hereafter. Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
For that man whom these do not trouble, O bull among men—
The steadfast one who is equal in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality. There is no being of the non-existent, nor is there non-being of the existent;
the end of both has been perceived by the seers of reality.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.
These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal embodied self.
It is indestructible and immeasurable; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not kill, nor is it killed.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to exist hereafter. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient is this [Self].
It is not slain when the body is slain. He who knows this Self as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable—
how, O Pārtha, can that person cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone?
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new,
even so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other [bodies].
The embodied soul passes into other new bodies;
weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it,
water does not moisten it, and wind does not dry it.
This [Self] is neither to be cut, nor to be burned, nor to be moistened, nor to be dried;
it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable.
Therefore, knowing this to be so, you ought not to grieve. Moreover,
even if you consider him to be constantly born or constantly dying,
even then, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for him.
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Therefore, regarding this inevitable matter, you ought not to grieve.
O Bhārata, beings have the unmanifest as their beginning and the manifest as their middle.
Their dissolution is indeed unmanifest; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Someone beholds this [Self] as a marvel, and likewise another speaks of it as a marvel.
And another hears this as something wonderful; yet even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it. This embodied soul, O Bhārata, is eternally indestructible within the body of everyone.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve for all beings;
moreover, considering your own duty, you ought not to waver,
for there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war.
"O Pārtha, happy are the Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this, which comes of its own accord and is an open door to heaven. But if you do not engage in this righteous war..."
Therefore, by abandoning your own duty and fame, you will incur sin; moreover, people will speak of your undying infamy. And for one who has been highly esteemed, infamy is worse than death.

The great chariot-warriors will think that you have desisted from the battle out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will now meet with contempt. Furthermore, your enemies will utter many unspeakable words against you.
They will revile your prowess; what indeed could be more painful than that?
Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle.

Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, then engage in battle; thus you shall not incur sin. This wisdom has been declared to you from the standpoint of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] from the standpoint of Yoga.
O Pārtha, endowed with that intellect by which you shall cast off the bondage of action;
in this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
for even a small measure of this dharma protects one from great fear.

O joy of the Kurus, in this world the intellect characterized by resolute determination is one; for the intellect of those lacking such determination is indeed many-branched and infinite. This flowery speech which the unwise proclaim—
O Pārtha, those who delight in the ritualistic declarations of the Vedas, who argue that there is nothing else,

whose souls are possessed by desire, and who look toward heaven as their goal— [they perform rituals] which yield birth as the fruit of action and abound in various specific rites directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power.

For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [attachment], the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative concentration. The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; O Arjuna, become free from the three qualities.
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the desire for acquisition and preservation, and self-possessed—
whatever purpose there may be in a small reservoir when there is a flood of water everywhere,
that much alone is the purpose of all the Vedas for the Brahmin who possesses true knowledge.
Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
Established in yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment.
Becoming the same in success and failure—this equanimity is called yoga.
For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in wisdom, for those who act for the sake of results are pitiable.
One who is endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds here in this world;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in action. For the wise, being endowed with wisdom, abandon the fruit born of action.

Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state that is free from suffering. When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what has been heard and what remains to be heard.
"When your intellect, which has been perplexed by the various scriptural teachings, stands firm and unshakable in concentrated absorption, then you will attain yoga. Arjuna said:

"What is the description of one whose wisdom is established, who is situated in samādhi, O Keśava? How does the one of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move? The Blessed One said:
When one abandons all desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha,

and is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom. One whose mind is unperturbed in sorrows and who is free from longing amidst pleasures— [is called steadfast].
Free from passion, fear, and anger, he is called a sage of steady wisdom.
He who is without attachment everywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious— his wisdom is firmly established.

And when he withdraws these senses from the objects of the senses in every way, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established. The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food.
Even his taste for objects ceases upon seeing the Supreme;
for, O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind of even a wise man who strives [to control them].
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. In a person who dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born.
From anger comes delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory. From the loss of memory comes the destruction of discernment, and from the destruction of discernment, one perishes.

But he who moves among sense-objects with his senses free from attachment and aversion, self-controlled and with his mind disciplined, attains serenity. In serenity, the destruction of all his sufferings arises.
For the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes established;
indeed, there is no wisdom for the undisciplined, nor is there meditative cultivation for the undisciplined.
For one who does not practice cultivation there is no peace, and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness?
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses,
it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him by whom [the senses] have been restrained in every way...
The wisdom of one whose senses are withdrawn from the objects of the senses is firmly established.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness,
even so do all desires enter him.
He attains peace, not the seeker of desires; that man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing,
without the sense of "mine," and without egoism— he attains peace.
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Established even at the time of death in this state, one attains the beatitude of Brahman.
Arjuna said:
If you consider intelligence to be superior to action, O Janārdana,
then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava? With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my mind.
"Therefore, tell me with certainty that one [path] by which I may attain the highest good.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O sinless one, in this world, a twofold path was declared by me of old."

For the followers of Sāṃkhya, it is through the yoga of knowledge; for the practitioners of Yoga, it is through the yoga of action. A person does not attain freedom from action by merely abstaining from actions, nor does he achieve perfection simply through renunciation.
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of nature.
He who sits restraining the organs of action while dwelling upon them with the mind [is deluded].
One whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called a hypocrite. But he who, O Arjuna, restraining the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is superior.
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the maintenance of the body would not be possible through inaction. This world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
In the beginning, the Lord of Creatures, having created all beings together with sacrifice, said:
"By this shall you propagate; let this be the cow of plenty that grants your desires."
By this [sacrifice], nourish the gods, and let those gods nourish you.
Nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good. For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire.

He who enjoys what has been given by them without first giving to them is indeed a thief. The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins; but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake alone eat only sin.
From food all beings come into being; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice comes rain; and sacrifice originates from action.
Know that action arises from Brahman, and Brahman arises from the Imperishable.

Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice. He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion here on earth— sinful in nature and delighting in the senses, O Pārtha, he lives in vain.
But the man who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self,
and who is content in the Self alone— for him there is no duty to be performed.
For him there is no purpose whatsoever here in this world through action, nor any at all through inaction.
And he has no dependence on any object whatsoever among all beings.
Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone; you should also act, having regard for the maintenance of the world. Whatever a great man does, that very same thing other people do.

Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that. O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by Me; there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage unweariedly in action at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect;
these worlds would perish if I were not to perform action.

I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these creatures. As the ignorant act with attachment to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.

One who is disciplined and acting with wisdom should not cause a confusion of intellect among the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all actions while performing them himself.
For it is by the qualities of *prakṛti* that all actions are performed in every way.
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. But the knower of truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the distinction between the qualities and their functions,
does not become attached, realizing that it is the qualities acting upon the qualities.
Those deluded by the qualities of *prakṛti* become attached to the actions of those qualities;
one who knows the Whole should not unsettle those dull-witted people who do not know the Whole.
Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self, [one should work].
"Free from desire and free from the sense of 'mine,' fight, rid of all feverish anxiety. Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine,
full of faith and free from cavil— they too are liberated from the bonds of action."
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, mindless, and lost. Even a man of wisdom acts in accordance with his own nature.
Beings follow their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of each sense-organ;
one should not come under their sway, for they are one's adversaries.
Better is one’s own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed. Death in one’s own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear.
Arjuna said:
"Then by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?
The Blessed Lord said:

This desire, this anger, born of the quality of passion (rajas), is all-consuming and greatly sinful; know it here as the enemy. Just as fire is covered by smoke and a mirror by dust, so is this [wisdom] covered.
Just as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so is this [knowledge] enveloped by that;
knowledge is enveloped by this eternal enemy of the wise,
O son of Kuntī, which takes the form of desire and is like an insatiable fire.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge. Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses.
Abandon this evil which destroys knowledge and realization. They say that the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses;
the intellect is superior to the mind; and he who is beyond the intellect is superior even to that.
Thus, having known that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by the Self,
O mighty-armed one, slay the enemy in the form of desire, who is difficult to overcome.
The Blessed Lord said:
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Thus, transmitted through this lineage, the royal seers have known it.
O scorcher of the foe, after a long time this yoga was lost here on earth;
that very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today,
for you are My devotee and My friend, and this is indeed the supreme secret.
Arjuna said:
Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier;
how then am I to understand that you spoke [this] in the beginning?
The Blessed Lord said:
Many births of mine have passed away, as well as yours, O Arjuna.
I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own creative power (māyā).
For whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata...
Whenever there is a resurgence of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself for the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, age after age.

He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, upon leaving the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to me, O Arjuna. Those whose passion, fear, and anger have departed, who are absorbed in me, and who have taken refuge in me—

Many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained my state. In whatever way people surrender unto me, in that same way do I reward them; O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.
Desiring the success of their actions, people here worship the gods;
for in the world of men, success born of action comes quickly.
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the divisions of qualities and actions.

Know Me to be the author of that [action] as well, yet the non-agent and immutable. Actions do not taint Me, nor do I have any desire for the fruits of action. He who thus recognizes Me is not bound by actions.

Knowing this, even the seekers of liberation of old performed action; therefore, you too perform action, which was performed by those of old even before them. Even the wise are bewildered as to what is action and what is inaction.

I shall declare to you that action, knowing which you will be liberated from evil. For one must understand action, and one must understand what is contrary to action, and one must understand inaction; the way of action is profound.
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. He whose undertakings are all free from desire and purposeful intent—
The wise call him a sage whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent,
he does nothing at all even though fully engaged in action.

Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action of the body alone, he incurs no sin. Satisfied with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy;
Being equanimous in success and failure, even though he acts, he is not bound. For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, his entire karma is completely dissolved.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is thus absorbed in the yoga of action consisting of Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained.
Other yogis worship sacrifice as the divine alone.
Others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman;
others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
and others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge;
likewise, others perform sacrifices of material objects, sacrifices of austerity, and sacrifices of yoga.
And ascetics of rigid vows, whose sacrifice is study and knowledge,

offer the outgoing breath into the incoming breath; others likewise offer the incoming breath into the outgoing breath, having restrained the movements of both the prāṇa and apāna, being solely devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Others, restricted in their food, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose sins have been destroyed by sacrifice. Partaking of the nectar that remains from the sacrifice, they go to the eternal Brahman.
This world is not for one who does not sacrifice; how much less another, O best of the Kurus?
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action, and knowing this, you shall be liberated.
O scorcher of foes, a sacrifice of knowledge is superior to a sacrifice performed with material objects;
for all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
Know that [knowledge] by prostration, by inquiry, and by service.
The wise who perceive the truth will instruct you in that knowledge,
O Pāṇḍava, by knowing which you shall no longer fall into such delusion; through it,
you shall see all beings without exception within yourself and then within me.
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone,
O Arjuna, just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes.
Just as a blazing fire reduces all fuel to ashes, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
Indeed, nothing so purifying as knowledge is found here in this world;
one who is perfected in yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
The man of faith, who is devoted to it and has his senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace before long.
But the ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish.

Neither this world nor the next exists, nor happiness, for one whose mind is full of doubt. O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been severed by knowledge, and who is established in the Self.
Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart, which has arisen from ignorance, take refuge in yoga and arise, O Bhārata!
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and yet again you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better.
The Blessed Lord said:
Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good;
however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
He who neither hates nor desires should be known as a perpetual renunciant.
For one who is free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is easily released from bondage.
The ignorant, but not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
even by being established in only one of them correctly, one obtains the fruit of both.
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the followers of Yoga. He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to achieve without Yoga.
The sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman before long.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, he is not tainted.
Even while seeing,
hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing,
speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, or closing his eyes, the disciplined knower of reality should think: "I do nothing at all."

Holding the conviction that "the senses move among the objects of the senses," he who performs actions by offering them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

Yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification. One who is disciplined, having renounced the fruit of action, attains peace that is final.
The undisciplined person, acting according to desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.
Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied being dwells in happiness within the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done.

The Lord creates neither the agency nor the actions of the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is nature that operates. The all-pervading Lord does not take upon Himself the sin or even the merit of anyone.
Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded. But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge, like the sun, reveals the Supreme.
With their intellects fixed on That, with their selves absorbed in That, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal,

those whose impurities have been washed away by knowledge go to the state from which there is no return. [They do so] toward a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, toward a cow, and toward an elephant.
The wise look with an equal eye upon a dog and even a dog-eater; for those whose minds are established in equality, rebirth is conquered even here.
For Brahman is indeed faultless and equal; therefore, they are established in Brahman.

One who has attained firm wisdom, being undeluded, knowing Brahman and established in Brahman, should neither rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant nor be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant. With his self unattached to external contacts, he finds that happiness which is in the Self.
With his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the wombs of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them.

That man who is able here, even before the release from the body, to endure the impulse arising from desire and anger— he is disciplined, he is happy. He who finds happiness within, whose recreation is within, and likewise whose light is solely within—

That yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction of Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇa*). The seers whose taints are exhausted attain the extinction of Brahman— those who have severed duality, who are self-controlled, and who delight in the welfare of all beings.
For those ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained,
and who have realized the Self, the extinction of Brahman is present on all sides.
Having turned outward sensory contacts away and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, one should remain with the vital breaths suspended within the mouth.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils, the sage who has restrained his senses, mind, and intellect, and who is intent upon liberation—
free from desire, fear, and anger— he is indeed liberated forever.
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. The Blessed Lord said:

He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi; he is not one who merely maintains no sacred fire, nor one who performs no action.
Know that what they call renunciation, O Pāṇḍava, is itself yoga.
For no one indeed becomes a yogin without having renounced all purposeful intent (saṃkalpa). For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once established in yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.

For when one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitional thoughts, then one is said to have ascended to yoga. One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not degrade the self.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. The self is the friend of that self by which the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who lacks self-mastery, the self itself would behave as an enemy toward the self.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is fully composed within,
amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor; such a person,
whose soul is satisfied by knowledge and realization, remains steadfast with senses subdued.
The yogi who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal is said to be disciplined;
he who possesses an even mind toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen, as well as toward the virtuous and the sinful, is preeminent.
The yogi, staying in solitude alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline himself;
having established his own firm seat in a clean place.
Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kusha grass,
one should sit upon that seat, making the mind one-pointed and restraining the activities of the mind and senses, and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady,
gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around at the directions, with a tranquil mind, free from fear, and established in the vow of celibacy— BhG 6.13–14a.
Restraining the mind, with his thoughts fixed on Me, disciplined and devoted to Me as the supreme goal, the yogi who thus constantly yokes his self, with his mind controlled,
attains the peace that culminates in liberation and abides in Me.
Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all;
nor for him who is addicted to excessive sleep, nor for him who is ever awake, O Arjuna.
Yoga belongs to one who is moderate in food and recreation, and disciplined in his actions.
For one who is disciplined in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering. When the well-restrained mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be "yoked."
As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile taught for the yogi of restrained mind who practices the yoga of the Self;
wherein the mind, stilled by the practice of yoga, comes to rest.
And where, seeing the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the self;
that absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses,
wherein established, one does not deviate from reality— [that state is yoga].
That which, having obtained it, one considers no other gain to be superior;
wherein established, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering—
let that be known as the severance of the union with suffering, designated as yoga.
That yoga must be practiced with firm resolve and an undiscouraged mind,
having abandoned all desires born of volitional thought without exception,
and having restrained the entire collection of the senses from every side by means of the mind alone.
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having fixed the mind upon the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, [one should restrain it].

Restraining it from there and there, he should bring it under control within the Self alone. For supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from blemish.
Thus constantly yoking the self, the yogi, freed from taint,
easily attains the infinite bliss that is the touch of Brahman.
[He perceives] the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self.
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives with equal vision everywhere;
he who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me.

He who, established in unity, worships Me as dwelling in all beings— that yogi, though engaged in any manner of conduct, dwells in Me. O Arjuna, he who sees with equanimity everywhere by means of the analogy of his own self—
Whether in happiness or in suffering, that yogi is considered supreme.
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, this yoga which has been taught by you through equanimity—
Because of its restlessness, I do not see a steady stability for it.
For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind.
The Blessed One said:
"Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control through practice and dispassion."
"Yoga is difficult to attain by one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my view.
But it can be attained through the proper means by one who strives with a controlled self.
Arjuna said:
"One who lacks perseverance, yet is endowed with faith, whose mind has strayed from yoga— having failed to attain perfection in yoga, O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does he go to?
Having fallen from both, does he not perish like a scattered cloud?"
O mighty-armed one, I am without support and utterly bewildered on the path of Brahman.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to dispel this doubt of mine completely;
for indeed, no one other than you is capable of cutting through this doubt.
The Blessed One said: O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him;
for no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state.
Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, one who has fallen from yoga is reborn in the home of the pure and the prosperous;
or else, he is born into a family of wise yogis themselves.
For such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in this world. Therein, he regains the mental disposition belonging to his former body,
and from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even further toward perfection.
By that very same prior practice, he is indeed drawn forward even against his will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.
But the yogi who strives with effort, having purified all taints, [attains perfection].

Having attained perfection through many births, he then goes to the supreme goal. The yogi is considered superior to the ascetics, even superior to the men of knowledge, and superior to the men of action; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.
Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me,
full of faith— he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Pārtha, with your mind attached to me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in me,
hear how you shall know me fully and without doubt. I shall declare to you this knowledge, together with realized wisdom (vijñāna), in its entirety.

Having known which, nothing further remains here to be known. Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
and ego— this is my material nature (prakṛti) divided eightfold. But know that there is another, higher nature of mine, distinct from this.
O mighty-armed one, know that I am the life-force by which this world is sustained; all beings have this as their source. I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. I am the taste in water, O son of Kuntī, and I am the radiance in the moon and the sun.
I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, and the virility in men; I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the radiance in fire;
I am the life-force in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid. And I am the strength of the strong, free from the taint of desire and passion.

I am desire in beings that is not contrary to dharma, O bull of the Bharatas. Know that all states of being—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.

Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*), this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable. For this divine illusion (*māyā*) of Mine, composed of the qualities, is difficult to overcome.
Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me;
their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, and they have resorted to a demonic nature.

O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. Among them, the man of wisdom, who is ever-steadfast and devoted to the One alone, is preeminent.

For I am exceedingly dear to the knower of wisdom, and he is dear to Me. All these [others] are indeed noble, but the man of wisdom I consider to be My very Self; for, with a disciplined mind, he is established in Me alone as the supreme goal.
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in me, realizing that "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled person is very rare.
Those whose wisdom has been swept away by various desires take refuge in other deities.
Adhering to their respective disciplines, constrained by their own natures,
whatever form each devotee desires to worship with faith,
I make that very faith of theirs steadfast.
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity],
and from that he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by me alone. But the fruit of those who possess little intelligence is finite.

The worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me as well. The unintelligent, not knowing my supreme nature—which is imperishable and unsurpassed—imagine me to have attained manifestation when I am actually unmanifest.
I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my yoga-māyā; deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable. I know the past and the present, O Arjuna.
And as for future beings, no one knows Me;
O Bharata, O scorcher of foes, all beings fall into delusion at the time of birth due to the confusion caused by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion.

But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end— they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites and firm in their vows, worship me. Those who, having taken refuge in me, strive for liberation from old age and death;

They know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action in its entirety; those who know Me, along with the elemental (adhibhūta), the divine (adhidaiva), and the sacrificial (adhiyajña), they—
possessing concentrated minds— know Me even at the time of death.
Arjuna said:
O Supreme Person, what is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma)?
And what is declared to be the elemental (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine (adhidaiva)?
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?
The Blessed Lord said:

The imperishable, supreme Brahman is called the Self (adhyātma), which is one's own nature. The creative emission that brings about the origin of the existence of beings is designated as action (karman).
The perishable state is the objective world (adhibhūta), and the Person (puruṣa) is the presiding deity (adhidaivata).

I myself am the sacrifice here in this body, O best of embodied beings. And at the time of death, he who departs casting off the body while remembering me alone attains my own state; there is no doubt in this.

Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, for one’s mind is constantly permeated by that state. Therefore, at all times remember Me and fight.
With your mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt;
by means of a mind disciplined through the yoga of practice and not wandering elsewhere,
O Pārtha, you go to the supreme, divine Person as you meditate upon Him.
He who meditates upon the ancient Seer, the Teacher,
subtler than the subtle,
the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable;
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga, [one should meditate on] that which is of solar radiance, beyond darkness.
Having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows,
he attains that divine Supreme Person,
whom those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable.
That goal which ascetics free from passion enter,
and desiring which they lead the life of celibacy—
that goal I shall declare to you in brief.
Restraining all the gates of the body, confining the mind within the heart,
and fixing one's vital breath in the head, established in the practice of yoga,
uttering the single-syllabled Brahman "Om" and remembering Me;
He who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. O Pārtha, for that ever-disciplined yogi who constantly and perpetually remembers me with undistracted mind, I am easily attained.

Having attained Me, those great-souled ones who have reached the supreme perfection do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering. O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return.

But having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist. Those people who know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas— they are the ones who truly understand day and night.
At the arrival of day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very same state known as the unmanifest.
This same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves away.

O Pārtha, at the coming of night he helplessly dissolves, and at the coming of day he comes forth again. But beyond that unmanifest state there is another, unmanifest and eternal being which does not perish even when all beings perish.

He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they say he is the supreme goal, that abode of mine reaching which they do not return. That is the Supreme Person, O Pārtha, who is attainable by unswerving devotion alone.
In whom all beings dwell, by whom all this is pervaded— O bull of the Bharatas, I shall declare that time at which departing yogis go either to non-return or to return.
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—
departing during these, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman. Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern solstice.
Having attained the lunar light there, the yogi returns. These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be the eternal courses of the world;
by the one, a person goes to non-return, and by the other, he returns again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna—
[even] in the Vedas, in sacrifices, and in austerities.
Having understood all this, the yogi transcends whatever fruit of merit is prescribed for acts of giving and attains the supreme, primordial abode.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall declare to you, who are free from malice, this most secret knowledge together with realized wisdom (vijñāna), by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil.
This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, this supreme purifier,
which is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable.
O scorcher of foes, men who have no faith in this dharma...
Failing to reach Me, they return to the path of the cycle of death. Pervaded by Me in My unmanifest form is this entire world; all beings dwell in Me, yet I do not dwell in them.

And yet the beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga! My Self, the source of all beings, sustains all beings but does not dwell in them, just as the great wind, though omnipresent, eternally remains in space.
In the same way, understand that all beings abide in Me.
O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa, all beings enter My own nature;
then, at the beginning of a new kalpa, I send them forth again.
"Taking hold of My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature;
yet those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya."
Sitting as if indifferent, unattached to those actions,
by Me as the supervisor, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. Their hopes are vain, their actions are fruitless, their knowledge is futile, and they are devoid of discernment.

They have taken refuge in the delusive nature of the Rākṣasas and Asuras. But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings.
Constantly glorifying me, striving with firm vows,
and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined.
Others also, sacrificing by means of the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me.
As oneness and as multiplicity, manifold and facing every direction—
I am the ritual act, I am the sacrifice, I am the ancestral offering, and I am the medicinal herb; I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather;
I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and indeed the Rig, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas.
I am the goal, the supporter, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend.
I am the origin, the dissolution, the support, the storehouse, and the imperishable seed. I give heat; I withhold and send forth the rain.
I am both immortality and death, O Arjuna, and both being and non-being.

Those who know the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven; having reached the holy world of the lord of the gods, they enjoy celestial pleasures.
In heaven they enjoy divine celestial pleasures;
having enjoyed that vast heavenly world,
when their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal realm.

Thus, those who have followed the dharma of the three Vedas obtain the state of going and returning, desiring their objects of desire. But those people who worship Me, thinking of no other, meditate upon Me.
For those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide their acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema). Even those who, endowed with faith, worship other deities,
they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.
For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall. Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors.

Those who worship the beings go to the beings; those who sacrifice to me also come to me. Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water one offers to me with devotion, that which is presented with devotion by the self-restrained soul, I accept.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī— perform all that as an offering unto Me.
In this way, you shall be liberated from the bonds of action, which yield both auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
With your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, you shall be liberated and come to Me.
(9.28c) I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear. (9.29a) But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I am also in them. (9.29c)
Even if one of very wicked conduct worships me with undivided devotion,
he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved. He quickly becomes a soul of dharma and attains eternal peace.

O son of Kuntī, declare it with certainty: my devotee never perishes. For even those who may be of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in me, O Pārtha.
How much more so, then, the meritorious Brahmins, my devotees, and likewise the royal sages!
Having reached this transient and unhappy world, worship me. Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me.
Thus, having disciplined yourself and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone.
The Blessed Lord said:
O mighty-armed one, listen again to My supreme word.
That which I shall declare to you, who are dear to Me, out of a desire for your welfare—
neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know My origin,
for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect.
He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds— he,
undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins.
Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility;
Happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence, fear and fearlessness,
non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame and infamy—
these various states of beings arise from Me alone.

The seven great seers of old, as well as the four Manus, were born of my own nature from my mind; from them these creatures in the world have descended. He who knows in truth this majesty and this yoga of mine—
He is united with unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt. Realizing that "I am the source of all, from me everything proceeds," the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me.

With their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they are satisfied and find delight. For those who are ever-devoted and worship me with love—

I bestow that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me. Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
Arjuna said:
You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest purity;
you are the eternal, divine Person, the primal God, unborn and all-pervading.
"All the sages say this of you, as do the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa; and you yourself tell it to me.
All this that you speak to me, O Keśava, I consider to be the truth."
O Blessed One, neither the gods nor the demons know Your manifestation;
You alone, O Supreme Person, know Yourself by Yourself,
O Creator of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods, Master of the world.
You ought to describe, without omission, Your divine self-manifestations (vibhūtis),
by which manifestations You abide pervading these worlds.
O Yogi, how may I know You by constantly meditating upon You?
In what various entities, O Blessed One, are You to be meditated upon by me? O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of Your own yoga and majesty;
for there is no satiety for me as I hear this nectar.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Very well, O best of the Kurus, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations in their principal forms; there is no end to my full extent."
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings;
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminous bodies I am the radiant Sun.
Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.
Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods I am Vāsava.
Among the senses I am the mind; among living beings I am consciousness.

Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth; among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among peaked mountains, I am Meru. And know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the foremost among the priests.
Among army commanders I am Skanda; among bodies of water I am the ocean.
Among great seers I am Bhṛgu; among words I am the single syllable Om.
Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of silent recitation; among immovable things I am the Himalayas.
Among all trees I am the Aśvattha; among divine seers, Nārada;
among Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among perfected beings, the sage Kapila.
Know me, O best of the Bharatas, to be Uccaiḥśravas among horses, born of the nectar of immortality.

Among the lordly elephants I am Airāvata, and among men I am the king; among weapons I am the thunderbolt, and among cows I am the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk. I am Kandarpa, the progenitor, and among serpents I am Vāsuki.
Among the Nāgas, I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa.
Among the ancestors, I am Aryaman; among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama. Among the Daityas, I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon time, I am Kāla.
Among beasts I am the king of beasts, and among birds I am the son of Vinatā;
I am the wind among purifiers, and Rāma among those who bear weapons;
among fish I am the makara, and among rivers I am the Ganges.
O Arjuna, I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations;
among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātmavidyā); and among those who debate, I am the argument.
Among letters, I am the letter ‘A’, and among compounds, I am the copulative compound (dvandva).
I alone am inexhaustible time; I am the Ordainer with faces turned in every direction.
I am death that carries all away, and I am the source of those who are yet to be. Among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness, and forgiveness.
Among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters, I am the Gāyatrī. Among months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, I am the flower-bearing spring.
Among deceivers, I am gambling; among the radiant, I am splendor itself.
I am victory; I am resolve; I am the goodness of those who possess goodness. Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, I am Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages, I am Vyāsa; among the poets, I am Uśanas the poet.
I am the rod of those who punish, and I am the policy of those who seek victory;
I am silence among secrets, and I am the knowledge of those who possess knowledge. And that which is the seed of all beings, O Arjuna, that too am I.
There is no being, whether moving or stationary, that exists without me. O scorcher of foes, there is no end to my divine manifestations;
this detailed account of my glory has been declared by me only in brief.
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, splendor, or power, know that to be born from but a fragment of my glory. Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge to you, O Arjuna?
Pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world.
Arjuna said:
For the sake of my grace, You have declared this supreme secret known as the Adhyātma.

By the words which You have spoken, this delusion of mine has vanished. For I have heard from You in detail, O lotus-eyed one, the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as Your imperishable majesty.
“O Supreme Lord, it is even as you have said concerning yourself;
O Supreme Person, I desire to see your divine form.
If you think it possible for me to behold it, O Lord, [then show it to me].”
"O Lord of Yoga, therefore show me Your imperishable Self.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Behold, O Pārtha, My forms by the hundreds and by the thousands."
Behold the various divine forms of manifold colors and shapes;
behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts—
many wonders never seen before, O Bhārata.

Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and unmoving beings situated here in one place within my body; and whatever else you wish to see. But you are not able to see me with this, your own physical eye.
"I give you a divine eye; behold my sovereign yoga.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great Lord of Yoga, then—
He revealed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form,
possessing many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders,
adorned with many divine ornaments, and wielding many uplifted divine weapons.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, the God consists of every wonder—endless and facing in all directions.
Suppose the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky; [such would be the radiance of that Being].
If that light were similar to the light of that Great-Souled One,
then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld the entire universe, divided manifoldly, situated within the body of the God of gods.
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end,
bowed his head to the God and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Arjuna said:
O God, I see all the gods within Your body,
as well as the hosts of various beings,
and Brahmā, the Lord seated upon his lotus throne.
I see all the ṛṣis and the divine serpents; I see you on every side with infinite forms, possessing many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes.
O Lord of the Universe, O You of Universal Form, I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning;
I see You wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus.
I see you as a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to behold from every direction,
with the brilliance of a flaming fire and the sun, immeasurable.
You are to be known as the supreme Imperishable;
you are the ultimate refuge of this universe;
you are the undecaying protector of the eternal Dharma.
You are considered by me to be the eternal Puruṣa,
without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power,
with infinite arms, and with eyes like the moon and the sun.
I see you with faces like blazing fires,
scorching this entire universe with your own splendor;
for you fill this space between heaven and earth.
All directions are pervaded by you alone;
having seen this wondrous and fierce form of yours,
O Great-Souled One, the three worlds are trembling with fear.
For these hosts of gods are entering into you;
some, terrified, praise you with palms joined;
and the hosts of great seers and perfected beings, having cried "Hail!", [offer their salutations].
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās— all these praise you with abundant hymns of praise.
The hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras,
and Siddhas all gaze upon you in amazement; they behold your great form with its many mouths and eyes.
O mighty-armed one, having seen [you] with many arms, thighs, and feet,
with many bellies, and terrible with many tusks,
the worlds as well as I am deeply distressed.
Having seen You touching the sky, blazing, multicolored,
with wide-open mouths and glowing, vast eyes,
my inner self is indeed deeply distressed.
O Viṣṇu, I find neither steadfastness nor peace upon merely beholding your mouths, which are terrible with tusks and resemble the fire of cosmic destruction.
I know not the directions, nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe!
And here are these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
All together with the hosts of kings—
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karṇa),
as well as our own leading warriors.
They are entering your mouths,
which are terrifying and formidable with tusks;
some are caught between the teeth.
They are seen with their heads crushed,
like the many currents of rivers rushing headlong toward the ocean.
In this way, these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths,
just as moths enter a kindled fire.
Just as rivers with full force enter the ocean for its destruction,
so too do these worlds, with full force, enter your mouths for their own destruction.
You lick up and devour the entire world on all sides with your blazing mouths,
filling the whole universe with your splendors.
O Viṣṇu, your fierce radiance scorches me;
tell me who you are, you of such terrible form.
Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious.
I desire to know you, the Primeval One;
for I do not comprehend your manifestation.
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown powerful;
I have begun here to gather in the worlds.
Even without you, all shall cease to exist.
Those warriors who stand arrayed in the opposing ranks— therefore arise, win glory,
and having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
"These have already been slain by Me alone;
be merely an instrument, O Savyasācin—
[slay] Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Jayadratha."
Slay Karṇa and the other heroic warriors as well, who have already been slain by me; do not be distressed. Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard these words of Keśava,
the diadem-wearing Arjuna, trembling, joined his palms in reverence.
Having bowed down again to Kṛṣṇa,
Arjuna, trembling with fear and prostrating himself, spoke with a faltering voice. Arjuna said:
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by the proclamation of Your glory the world rejoices and is filled with devotion;
the demons flee in fear toward every direction.
All the hosts of perfected beings bow down to you;
and why should they not bow to you, O Great Soul,
who are greater even than Brahmā, the primordial creator?
O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe, you are the imperishable, that which is existent and non-existent, and that which is beyond them. You are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa.
You are the supreme repository of this universe;
you are the knower, the object of knowledge, and the highest abode.
By you, O Being of infinite forms, the entire universe is pervaded.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and the Moon;
you are Prajāpati and the Great-Grandfather. Homage, homage be to You a thousand times!
And again, yet once more, homage, homage to You! Homage to You from the front and from behind; let there be homage to You from every side, O All!
You possess infinite power and immeasurable valor;
you pervade all, and therefore you are everything.
Since I thought of you as a friend, I have spoken to you impulsively.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava,
O friend— because I did not know this majesty of yours, whether through negligence or even out of affection, [I have addressed you thus].
And when you were treated with disrespect for the sake of mockery— whether alone or in the presence of others, O Acyuta, during recreation, rest, sitting, or eating;
Therefore, I seek forgiveness from you, the immeasurable one.
You are the father of this world, both moving and unmoving;
you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher.
There is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone superior, O You of matchless power, even in the three worlds?
Therefore, having bowed down and prostrated my body;
I seek to propitiate you, the Lord worthy of praise—
just as a father for his son, or a friend for his friend;
O God, you who are dear, it is right that you should endure me, your beloved.
Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled;
yet my mind is agitated by fear.
O God, show me that very same form.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe!
I wish to see You just as before— wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with the discus in Your hand.
"By that very same four-armed form,
O thousand-armed one, become the universal-formed one!
The Blessed Lord said:
O Arjuna, being pleased with you, I have by my own power revealed this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primordial.
That which has never been seen by me before through anything other than you—
neither by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts,
nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities.
"O hero of the Kurus, it is not possible for anyone other than you to see me in such a form in the world of men.
Let there be no fear in you, nor let there be any state of confusion."
Having seen this terrible form of mine,
you are now free from fear and your mind is gladdened; behold once more this very same form of mine.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva again showed him his own form.
And the Great-Souled One, having again assumed a gentle form, comforted him who was terrified.
Arjuna said:
"Having seen this gentle human form of yours, O Janārdana,
I have now become composed in mind and have returned to my natural state.
The Blessed Lord said:
You have seen this form of mine which is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in this way.
It is indeed possible to see Me in such a form as you have seen Me;
but by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna,
can I be known and seen in this way in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe.
"He who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme goal, who is devoted to me, who is free from attachment,
and who is without enmity toward all beings— he comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
Arjuna said:
"Among those who, thus ever-devoted, worship you with devotion,
and those who worship the imperishable and unmanifest— the former, which group is most skilled in yoga?
The Blessed Lord said:
Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined.
But those who worship the Indestructible, the indefinable, the unmanifest—

Restraining the entire collection of the senses, with equal vision toward all, and devoted to the welfare of all beings, they attain Me alone— Me who am omnipresent, inconceivable, immutable, immovable, and eternal.

The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater; for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings. But those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are intent on Me—
Those who worship Me, meditating on Me with a yoga that is indeed single-minded,
for them— whose minds are absorbed in Me— I become the deliverer from the ocean of the mortal cycle of rebirth, O Pārtha, before long.
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me.
Then, from this moment forward, you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt. But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily upon Me, [then practice yoga].
Therefore, O Dhanañjaya, seek to attain Me by the yoga of constant practice. If you are unable even to practice, be intent on My work;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.

But if you are unable even to do this, take refuge in my yoga and then renounce the fruits of all actions with self-control. For knowledge is better than practice, and meditation is superior to knowledge.
From meditation comes the renunciation of the fruits of action; from renunciation, peace follows immediately.
One who is not hostile toward any living beings, but is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of "mine" and the ego, equal in pain and pleasure, and patient—[such a person attains peace].

The yogi who is ever contented, self-controlled, firm of resolve, and whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me— that devotee of Mine is dear to Me. He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world;
He who is free from joy, impatience, fear, and agitation— he is dear to Me. He who is indifferent, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress,
and has renounced all undertakings— that devotee of Mine is dear to Me.
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires,
who has renounced both good and evil, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to Me.
He who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as in honor and dishonor;
A person who remains equanimous amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, who is free from attachment,
for whom blame and praise are equal, who observes silence, who is content with whatever comes,
who has no fixed abode, whose mind is steady, and who is devoted to Me— that man is dear to Me.
But those who worship this nectar of dharma as it has been described,
full of faith, regarding Me as their supreme goal— those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me.
The Blessed Lord said:
O son of Kuntī, this body is called the *kṣetra* (field). Those who know this call him who understands it the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field).
And know me, O Bhārata, as the *kṣetrajña* in all fields.

The knowledge of the field and the knower of the field— that, in my view, is true knowledge. Hear from me in brief what that field is, of what nature it is, what its modifications are, from whence it arises, and who he (the knower) is, and what his powers are.
It has been sung in many ways by the seers in various distinct Vedic hymns,
and also in the definitive and reasoned words of the Brahma-sūtras:
"The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest alone."
The eleven organs, the five objects of the senses,
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field together with its modifications in brief.
Absence of pride, absence of hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, straightforwardness,
service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-restraint,
detachment from the objects of the senses, and also the absence of egoism.
The perception of birth, death, old age, disease, suffering, and defect;
lack of attachment and absence of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and the like;
and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the desirable and the undesirable.
Unswerving devotion to Me through the yoga of non-duality;
dwelling in solitary places; lack of delight in the assembly of men;
constancy in the knowledge of the Self; and perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality.
This is declared to be knowledge; ignorance is that which is otherwise than this.
I shall now proclaim that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality:
the beginningless Supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere;
it possesses ears everywhere in the world, and it stands pervading all. It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses.
