It is unattached yet the sustainer of all; devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities. It is both outside and inside all beings; it is both the unmoving and the moving. Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, and yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings;
it should be known as the sustainer of beings, as that which devours, and as that which brings forth.
It is said to be the light even of lights, beyond darkness.
"Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge reside in the heart of every being.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been briefly described.
My devotee, having realized this, attains to my own state of being.
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that all modifications and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti. In the state of being the agent of cause and effect, Prakṛti is said to be the cause.
The Puruṣa is said to be the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain;
for the Puruṣa, abiding in Prakṛti, experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti. Attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs.

The supreme person within this body is called the witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the great lord, and also the supreme self. He who thus knows the person along with primordial nature and its qualities—
Even acting in every way, he is not born again.
Some perceive the Self by means of the Self within the self through meditation;
others by means of the yoga of discernment (sāṃkhya), and still others by the yoga of action (karmayoga).
But others, not knowing thus, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, certainly cross over death.
Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving—
Know that, O bull of the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field. He who sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings,
undying amidst those that perish— he truly sees.

For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy the self by means of the self; thereby one attains the supreme goal. And all actions are being performed in every way by nature alone.
He who thus perceives the Self as the non-agent, he truly sees. When one perceives the manifold existence of beings as situated in the One,
and likewise their expansion from that alone, then one attains Brahman.
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this supreme Self is immutable;
O son of Kuntī, although dwelling within the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.
Just as space, being all-pervading, is not tainted because of its subtlety, so too is the Self.

Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so does the Lord of the Field (kṣetrī) illumine the entire field (kṣetra), O Bhārata; likewise, the Self (ātman), though abiding everywhere within the body, is not tainted.
Thus, those who perceive with the eye of knowledge the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, as well as the liberation from the material nature of beings, they go to the Supreme.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall further declare the supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge,
by knowing which all the sages have attained the highest perfection beyond this world. Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have come to possess a nature identical to mine.
Even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. My womb is the Great Brahman; in it I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs.
O son of Kuntī, whatever forms arise in all wombs, their great source is Brahman, and I am the father who provides the seed. Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities arise from Prakṛti.
O mighty-armed one, these qualities bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body.
Among them, *sattva*, because of its purity, is illuminating and free from affliction;
it binds, O sinless one, through attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge.
Know that *rajas* consists of passion, arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action.
Know, however, that *tamas* arises from ignorance, deluding all embodied beings.
It binds them through negligence, laziness, and sleep, O Bhārata.
Sattva attaches one to happiness; rajas, O Bhārata, to action;
but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence.
Overpowering both passion and darkness, goodness prevails, O Bhārata; likewise, passion overcomes goodness and darkness, and darkness overcomes goodness and passion.
When light arises through all the gates in this body, [it is the sign of goodness].
When knowledge arises, then one should know that *sattva* has increased.
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—
these arise when *rajas* has increased, O bull of the Bharatas.
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—
these arise when *tamas* has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
But when one who bears a body meets death while *sattva* has increased, [he attains the worlds of the knowers of Brahman].
Then, one attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest;
having met its dissolution in *rajas*, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in *tamas*, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.

They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by goodness (sattva); the fruit of passion (rajas) is suffering, and the fruit of darkness (tamas) is ignorance. From goodness arises knowledge, and from passion arises greed alone.

From *tamas* arise negligence, delusion, and ignorance itself. Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle; and those established in the activity of the lowest quality, *tamas*, go downward.
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities,
and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state. Having transcended these three qualities, which arise from the body, the embodied soul [is liberated].
Freed from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, he attains immortality.
Arjuna said:
"By what marks, O Lord, does one who has transcended these three qualities become known?"
"What is his conduct, and how does he transcend these three qualities?
The Blessed One said:
"O Pāṇḍava, [he transcends] illumination, activity, and indeed delusion."
He does not hate what has arisen, nor does he long for what has ceased;
sitting like one indifferent, he who is not shaken by the qualities remains steady, thinking,
"The qualities are merely operating," and does not waver.
Equanimous in pain and pleasure, established in self, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
the wise one is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, the same in blame and self-praise;
equal in honor and dishonor, and equal toward the parties of friend and foe.

He who has renounced all undertakings is said to have transcended the qualities. And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman.
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable,
of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. The Blessed Lord said:
They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below; the Vedas are its leaves—he who knows it is a knower of the Veda. Its branches extend below and above;
With their growth consisting of the *guṇas*, with objects of sense as their sprouts,
and with roots extending downward,
they are bound to action in the world of men.
Its form is not perceived here in such a way;
it has no end, no beginning, and no foundation.
This is the banyan tree with its deeply rooted roots.
Having severed [the bonds] with the firm weapon of non-attachment,
one must then seek that state,
reaching which they do not return again.
I take refuge in that very same Primeval Person,
from whom this ancient process has issued forth—
those who are free from pride and delusion, and who have conquered the defect of attachment.
Those who are established in the inner self, whose desires have ceased,
who are liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain—
those undeluded ones go to that imperishable state.

Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return. It is My very own eternal portion, which has become the individual soul in the world of living beings.
The Lord draws away the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their own nature;
when he acquires a body and when he departs from it,
he takes these with him and goes forth, just as the wind carries fragrances from their sources.
Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose, as well as the mind, this [Self] experiences the objects of the senses—
whether it is departing, remaining, or enjoying, endowed with the qualities.
The deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it. Striving yogis behold it as abiding within themselves;
yet even though they strive, those of unrefined self and lacking discernment do not see it.
That light which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world,
and that which is in the moon and in the fire— know that light to be mine. And entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital power.
Becoming the sap-filled moon, I nourish all plants;
and becoming the fire Vaiśvānara, residing within the bodies of living beings and joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the four kinds of food.
And I am seated within the heart of all;
from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known.
I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas alone.
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are the perishable; the one who stands firm is called the imperishable.
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (Paramātman),
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am even higher than the imperishable, [I am the Supreme Person].

Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). O Bhārata, he who knows Me thus, undeluded, as the Supreme Person, is all-knowing and worships Me with his whole being.
Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me.
Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that was to be done.
The Blessed Lord said:
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness;
non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of calumny; Bg 16.002a–b.
Compassion toward all beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty,
steadiness, vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and absence of excessive pride—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with the divine nature.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born for the demonic endowment.
The divine endowment leads to liberation; the demonic is considered to lead to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava; you are born into a divine nature.
There are two types of creation of beings in this world: the divine and the demonic.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic.
Demoniacal people do not understand the path of action nor the path of cessation;
in them there is neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth. They say that this world is without truth, without foundation, and without a Lord.
"Arising from one another, what else could this be but caused by desire?
Holding fast to this view, those ruined souls of small intellect,
intent on fierce deeds and harmful to the world, arise for its destruction.
Resorting to insatiable desire, and possessed of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, they act with impure vows, having grasped false notions through delusion;
and they are devoted to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death.
Regarding the enjoyment of desires as the ultimate goal and being convinced that "this is all," they are bound by hundreds of snares of hope; devoted to lust and anger,
they strive for the accumulation of wealth through unjust means for the sake of enjoying their desires.
"Today this has been gained by me; this desire I shall attain. This is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again.
That enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well."
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy;
I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance.
With minds distracted by many thoughts and enveloped by the net of delusion,
they are attached to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and fall into impure hell. Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride, they fall.
They perform sacrifices with ostentatious rites, out of hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions;
possessed by egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger,
they hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being full of malice.

Those hateful, cruel, and inauspicious lowest of men, I perpetually hurl into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence. Having entered demonic wombs, these deluded ones [wander] from birth to birth.
Without ever reaching Me, O son of Kuntī, they then go to the lowest state. This threefold gate to hell, which is the destroyer of the self—
lust, anger, and greed— one should therefore renounce these three.
Freed from these three gateways to darkness, O son of Kuntī,
a man practices what is for his own welfare and thereby attains the supreme goal.
But he who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims—
He attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.

Therefore, let the scripture be your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; having understood what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.

Arjuna said: O Kṛṣṇa, what is the firm foundation of those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, sacrifice while endowed with faith— is it goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)?
The Blessed Lord said:
"The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature;
it is sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic—listen to that."
The faith of every person, O Bhārata, conforms to their own nature;
this person is made of faith—whatever one’s faith is, that indeed one is.
Those of *sattva* worship the gods, while those of *rajas* worship the *yakṣas* and *rakṣasas*.
Other people, who are characterized by darkness (tāmasa), worship ghosts and hosts of spirits.
Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures, being possessed of hypocrisy and egoism, and driven by the force of desire and passion— Bhg_17.004c–005c; Bhg_17.005a–c.
Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements within the body,
and Me as well who dwell within the body— know them to be of demonic resolve. Furthermore, food is dear to everyone in three ways.
Sacrifice, austerity, and likewise charity—listen now to this distinction between them.
Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and satisfaction; which are savory, succulent, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—these are dear to those of sattvic nature.
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to those of the passionate nature (rājasa); they bring about pain, grief, and disease.
So too are stale, flavorless, putrid, and leftover food.
Food that is stale, as well as impure, is dear to those of tamasic nature. That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunctions by those who do not desire its fruits,
with the mind composed in the thought "the sacrifice must indeed be performed," is sattvic.

But that sacrifice which is performed, O best of the Bharatas, aiming for a fruit and even for the sake of ostentation— know that sacrifice to be rajasic. That which is devoid of rule, where food is not distributed, lacking mantras, and without sacrificial fees;
A sacrifice devoid of faith is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Reverence for the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—these are said to be austerity of the body.
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial,
as well as the practice of reciting sacred texts— this is called austerity of speech.
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, and self-restraint [are called austerity of the mind].
Purity of disposition— this is called mental austerity. That threefold austerity, when performed with supreme faith by disciplined men who do not desire fruits, is declared to be *sāttvika*.
Whatever austerity is performed for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, and with hypocrisy,
that is declared here in this world to be rajasic— fickle and unstable.
Whatever austerity is performed by means of a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself, [that is tamasic].
Or that which is given for the purpose of destroying another— that is declared to be tamasic.
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given," to one who does not return the favor,
at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient— that gift is remembered as sattvic.
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit,
and which is given with a sense of distress— that gift is considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients—
That which is offered without respect and with contempt is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
"Oṃ," "Tat," and "Sat"—this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman;
by means of this, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained in ancient times.
Therefore, having uttered "Om," the rites of sacrifice, gift-giving,
and austerity proceed constantly according to the prescribed rules for those who discourse on Brahman;
while with "Tat," one performs the rites of sacrifice and austerity without aiming for a fruit.

And various acts of giving are performed by those desiring liberation. The word *sat* is employed in the sense of "being" and in the sense of "goodness"; likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is used for a praiseworthy action.
Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called *sat* (the real);
and action performed for their sake is likewise designated as *sat*.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given in charity, or performed as austerity, if done without faith— [is called *asat*].
"O Pārtha, that is called 'unreal' (asat), for it exists neither after death nor here in this world.
Arjuna said:
"O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of renunciation (saṃnyāsa)."
And [tell me] separately, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin, about renunciation.
The Blessed Lord said:
The wise know the abandonment of actions performed for the sake of desire as *saṃnyāsa*.
The wise declare that renunciation is the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions. Some thinkers say that action should be abandoned as being full of fault;
others say that the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.
Hear from Me, O best of the Bharatas, the definitive conclusion regarding renunciation;
for renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds. The acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity must not be abandoned; they are indeed to be performed.

Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise. But even these actions, O Pārtha, must be performed after abandoning attachment and the desire for fruits; this is my firm and supreme conviction.
But the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate;
its abandonment out of delusion is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). If one should abandon action merely because it is painful, out of fear of physical exertion—

Having performed a renunciation that is characterized by passion (rājasa), one will not obtain the fruit of renunciation at all. O Arjuna, when obligatory action is performed simply because it ought to be done, having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
He who does not hate unwholesome action and is not attached to wholesome action—
he is a renouncer, pervaded by goodness, wise, and one whose doubts are severed.
For it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely.
But he who renounces the fruits of action is called a renouncer.
The threefold fruit of action— undesirable, desirable, and mixed—
accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.
O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes declared in the Sāṃkhya system of definitive conclusion for the successful accomplishment of all actions:
the locus, as well as the agent, and the various kinds of instruments.
And various distinct efforts, as well as destiny as the fifth;
whatever action a man undertakes with his body, speech, and mind—
whether it be righteous or its opposite— these five are its causes.
This being so, he who, due to an unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the sole agent— being of dull wit, he does not see.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not smeared [by attachment], [sees].
Even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound. Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulse to action.
The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action.

Knowledge, action, and the agent—these three are indeed described according to the distinction of the *guṇas* in the enumeration of the *guṇas*; hear them also as they truly are. By which one perceives the single, imperishable Being in all beings...
Know that knowledge to be *sāttvika* which perceives the undivided within the divided;
but know that knowledge to be *rājasa* which perceives various distinct entities as separate in all beings.
But that which is attached to a single task as if it were the whole, performed without regard for reason,
devoid of the true goal, and insignificant— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
That which is performed as a matter of duty, free from attachment, and without passion or hatred— [that is declared to be of the nature of goodness].

Action performed by one who does not desire its fruit is said to be *sāttvika*. But that action which is performed with a desire for reward, or again with egoism, and which involves great effort, is declared to be *rājasa*.
Action that is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity— that is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
One who is free from attachment, devoid of egoism, and endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm...
The agent who remains unchanged in success and failure is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
The agent who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure,
and possessed by joy and sorrow is proclaimed to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
The unrefined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, dishonest, lazy,
despondent, and procrastinating doer is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Now hear the threefold division of intelligence and fortitude according to the qualities (guṇas).
O Dhanañjaya,

that intellect which understands, in their entirety and with their distinctions, the path of action and the path of renunciation, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation— that intellect, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
That intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, O Pārtha, is rajasic.
That which, shrouded by darkness, considers adharma to be dharma is tamasic.

O Pārtha, that intellect which perceives all objects erroneously is tāmasī. O Pārtha, that resolve by which one maintains the functions of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through unwavering yoga is sāttvikī.

But that steadfastness, O Arjuna, by which one maintains dharma, pleasure, and wealth, while desiring their fruits through attachment— that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is rajasic. That [steadfastness] by which one holds fast to sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and even intoxication—
The dull-witted person does not relinquish it; that resolve, O Pārtha, is tāmasī.
Now hear from me, O bull of the Bharatas, about the threefold happiness, wherein one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering.
That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result, born from the clarity of one’s own intellect— that is declared to be *sāttvika*.
That which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects and is like nectar at first—
That pleasure which is like poison in its consequence is declared to be rajasic.
That pleasure which is delusive to the self both at the outset and in its aftermath,
arising from sleep, indolence, and negligence, is said to be tamasic.
There is no being on earth, nor again among the gods in heaven,
that is free from these three qualities born of material nature—
of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras, O scorcher of the foe.
Actions are divided according to the qualities born of one's own nature.
Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, uprightness,
knowledge, realization, and faith— these are the duties of a Brahmin, arising from his own nature.
Valor, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle,
as well as generosity and lordliness— these are the duties of a Kṣatriya, born of his own nature. Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and commerce are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature.
Service is the duty born of one's own nature even for the Śūdra. Devoted to their respective duties, a person attains perfection.
Listen now to how one who is intent on his own duty finds success.
From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—
by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. One’s own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed.
Performing action that is determined by one's own nature, one incurs no sin.
O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon innate action, even though it is possessed of fault;
for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, as fire is by smoke.
One whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has conquered the self, and from whom longing has departed,
attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of actionlessness. Learn from me how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman.
O son of Kuntī, in brief, this is the supreme culmination of knowledge:
being endowed with a purified intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude,
one abandons objects such as sound and casts aside passion and hatred.
Frequenting solitary places, eating light food, with speech, body, and mind restrained, constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation, and having fully taken recourse to dispassion,
[one should abandon] egoism, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated, free from the sense of "mine," and at peace, he is fit for becoming Brahman. Having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me.
Through devotion, one comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what My nature is. Then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter.
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who takes refuge in Me [attains this].

By my grace, one attains the eternal, imperishable state. Having surrendered all actions to me with the mind, regarding me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of discernment, always keep your mind fixed on me.
With your mind fixed on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace;
but if, out of egoism, you do not listen to Me, you shall perish.
If, relying on egoism, you think, "I will not fight," [you are mistaken].

This resolve of yours is false; nature will compel you. Bound by your own action born of your inherent nature, O son of Kuntī, that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, you shall do even against your will.
The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.
Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bharata.
"By His grace, you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than all secrets, been declared to you by Me. Reflect upon it in its entirety and do as you wish.
Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall speak what is for your benefit. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
"You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone.
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve."

This should never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is devoid of devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who finds fault with Me. But he who shall declare this supreme secret among My devotees—

Having offered supreme devotion to Me, he shall come to Me alone; of this there is no doubt. Among human beings, there is none who performs what is more pleasing to Me than he, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to Me than he.

And whoever shall request this righteous discourse between us, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. And even that man who hears it with faith and without malice, [shall attain the supreme goal].
He too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
O Pārtha, has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind?
O Dhanañjaya, has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed within you?
Arjuna said:
"O Acyuta, my delusion is destroyed and memory has been regained through your grace.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as you command."
Saṃjaya said:
Thus have I heard this wonderful dialogue, which causes the hair to stand on end, between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha.

O King, by the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret Yoga directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as he himself was speaking it; and remembering again and again this wonderful dialogue, I am filled with wonder.
I rejoice again and again in the merit of Keśava and Arjuna;
and remembering again and again that most wonderful form of Hari,
O King, great is my amazement, and I rejoice over and over.
Where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, is, and where Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, is, there prosperity, victory, wealth, and steadfast policy are certain; this is my conviction.
